bib.title: Bandit Algorithms, Chapter 6: The Explore-Then-Commit Algorithm

question: How should a stochastic k-armed bandit learner split rounds between exploring every arm a fixed number of times and committing to the empirically best arm, and what regret does that give?
contributions: Defines the explore-then-commit (ETC) policy (Algorithm 1) with exploration length m per arm
Theorem 6.1: finite-time regret bound for ETC on any 1-subgaussian bandit
Tuning of m for k=2 giving instance-dependent (6.6) and worst-case (6.7) bounds
Notes on anytime/doubling trick, epsilon-greedy and elimination, with exercises

results.claim: ETC regret on any 1-subgaussian k-armed bandit with 1<=m<=n/k is bounded by m*sum(gap_i) + (n-mk)*sum(gap_i*exp(-m*gap_i^2/4)); the proof uses a sqrt(2/m)-subgaussian difference of empirical means and Corollary 5.5.

results.claim: For k=2 with gap Delta, the Theorem 6.1 bound simplifies to m*Delta + n*Delta*exp(-m*Delta^2/4) (Eq 6.4); it is minimised up to rounding by m = max{1, ceil((4/Delta^2) log(n Delta^2/4))} (Eq 6.5) and then Rn <= min{n Delta, Delta + (4/Delta)(1+max{0, log(n Delta^2/4)})} (Eq 6.6).

results.claim: The tuned bound implies a worst-case (gap-free) bound Rn <= Delta + C*sqrt(n) with C a universal constant (left as Exercise 6.2); with Delta<=1 this is Rn <= 1 + C*sqrt(n).

limits: The tuned m in Eq 6.5 depends on the unknown gap Delta as well as on n; the chapter says it is seldom reasonable to assume the gap is known.
ETC is not anytime: the commitment time depends on the horizon; the doubling trick (Ex 6.6) fixes this.
All algorithms assume knowledge of the subgaussian constant (sigma=1 by normalisation).
Garivier et al. 2016b: ETC is necessarily suboptimal in the limit of infinite data (Chapter 16).
Worst-case bound is infinite without a bound on the reward range (Delta<=1).
Analysis is stated for k=2 when tuning m; Theorem 6.1 holds for k arms.
practices: Explore each arm exactly m times in round-robin order, then commit to argmax of the empirical mean for the remaining rounds (Algorithm 1, book p.92).
For k=2 set m = max{1, ceil(4/Delta^2 * log(n Delta^2/4))} when n and Delta are known (Eq 6.5).
If the gap is unknown, choose m from n alone for O(n^(2/3)) regret, or use a data-dependent stopping rule or an elimination algorithm (book p.94, Ex 6.5, 6.8).
Use the doubling trick to remove the need to know the horizon (Note 1, Ex 6.6).
epsilon-greedy is a randomised relative of ETC: play the empirically best arm with probability 1-eps_t, else a uniform random arm (Note 3, Ex 6.7).

terms.definition: explores by playing each arm a fixed number of times and then exploits by committing to the arm that appeared best during exploration
bounds that only depend on the horizon and class of bandits, not the specific instance
bounds like Eq 6.6 that depend on the suboptimality gap
an algorithm that does not require advance knowledge of the horizon n
a randomised relative of ETC that in round t plays the empirically best arm with probability 1-eps_t and otherwise explores uniformly at random
